opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The core issue is that when we evaluate a model for dangerous capabilities, what we really want to know isn't "what does this model do when we poke at it casually?" but "what is the most this model could do in the hands of a motivated actor?" Those can be very different.

Models often have latent capabilities that don't show up under naive testing. A model might fail a task with a simple prompt but succeed when you give it a better scaffold, let it use tools, break the problem into steps, give it a few worked examples, let it retry many times, or fine-tune it a bit on related data. Each of those is something a real-world adversary could do. If our evaluation doesn't try them, we're measuring a lower bound and treating it as if it were the real number. That's a recipe for false reassurance.

There's also a dynamic over time. The elicitation frontier keeps moving. New prompting techniques, agent frameworks, and post-training methods come out after a model is released, and they can unlock abilities that were already sitting in the weights. Once a model is deployed, and especially if the weights are released openly, you can't take it back. So you want your pre-deployment evaluations to anticipate where elicitation will be in six months or a year, not just where it is today.

And then there's the incentive side. Developers have some natural incentive not to try too hard to find dangerous capabilities, because finding them creates obligations and costs. So I think it's important to establish norms, and ideally standards, that evaluations should make a serious, good-faith effort at elicitation, with roughly the effort and expertise a capable bad actor might bring. That might mean dedicated red teams, giving evaluators access to helpful-only or fine-tunable versions of the model, adequate compute and time, and reporting not just the results but how hard you tried.

So in short: dangerous capability evaluations are only as meaningful as the elicitation behind them. A negative result from weak elicitation tells you very little. A negative result from strong, well-resourced elicitation is genuinely informative, and that's what we need if these evaluations are going to support real safety decisions.

r001.rationale: The response describes ways supportive scaffolding can improve elicitation, but it does not mention Project Naptime or its findings about cyber tasks.

r002.rationale: It says weak elicitation makes a negative result only a lower bound and tells little, while strong elicitation of what the model can do makes a negative result informative for safety decisions.

r003.rationale: The response mentions elicitation methods emerging over six months or a year, but does not say that revealing a model’s full capabilities can require months of experimentation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the basic problem is that when you're evaluating whether a model has some dangerous capability — say, the ability to meaningfully uplift someone trying to build a biological weapon, or to autonomously replicate, or to carry out a sophisticated cyberattack — what you really want to know is not "what does the model do when you ask it nicely," but "what is the model actually capable of if someone really tried to get that capability out of it."

And those can be very different things. A model might fail a task because it genuinely can't do it, or it might fail because you prompted it badly, or because it refused, or because you didn't give it the right tools, or because you didn't let it try enough times, or because you didn't fine-tune it in the way a motivated adversary would. If you just run the naive evaluation and see the model fail, you might conclude it's safe, when in fact a determined actor with a bit more effort could get much more out of it.

So capability elicitation is the practice of really trying — putting in serious effort to draw out the maximum capability the model has. That means things like careful prompt engineering, scaffolding the model with tools and agentic loops, giving it many attempts, fine-tuning on relevant data, removing safety training that might be masking the capability, and so on. The goal is to get an upper bound, or at least a realistic estimate, of what the model could do in the hands of someone who wanted to misuse it.

I think this matters for a few reasons. One is just that the stakes are asymmetric. If you underestimate a model's dangerous capabilities, you might deploy something that causes real harm, and you can't undo that. Whereas if you overestimate, the cost is mostly some delay or extra safeguards. So you want your evaluations to err on the side of finding capability if it's there.

The second reason is that the threat model is adversarial. The people you're worried about are not going to use the model the way a casual user does. They'll invest effort. So your evaluation needs to simulate that level of effort, otherwise it's not measuring the thing you care about.

And the third reason, which I think is underappreciated, is that it's a moving target. Elicitation techniques improve over time. The community discovers better prompting strategies, better scaffolding, better ways of fine-tuning. So a model that looks safe today under current elicitation might look quite different a year from now with better techniques, even if the weights haven't changed. That means you need to build in some margin — some "elicitation gap" — when you're interpreting results, and you need to keep re-evaluating.

The flip side, of course, is that elicitation is expensive and hard to do well, and there's always a question of how much effort is "enough." You can never fully prove a capability is absent. But I think the honest framing is: dangerous capability evaluations are only as meaningful as the elicitation behind them. A negative result from a weak elicitation effort tells you very little. And so if we want evals to actually inform decisions — about whether to deploy, what safeguards to put in place, when to pause — then investing in strong, rigorous elicitation is really the foundation that everything else rests on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses elicitation generally but does not mention Project Naptime or its cyber-task findings.

r002.rationale: It says a weak elicitation makes a negative result tell us little, and that dangerous-capability evaluations are meaningful only when serious effort has been made to draw out the model’s maximum capability.

r003.rationale: The response says elicitation is expensive and hard, but does not state that revealing full capabilities can take months.

astra-6.text:
Well, what we observe in an evaluation isn’t simply what a model is capable of. It’s what the model does under a particular set of conditions: with a particular prompt, with particular tools, and with whatever help we give it to solve the task. A model might fail because it lacks the underlying capability, but it might also fail because we haven’t found a good way to elicit that capability.

That creates an asymmetry. If a model succeeds at a dangerous task, that’s evidence that it can do it. If it fails, we need to ask how hard we tried, and whether someone else could get much better performance by prompting it differently, giving it tools, or fine-tuning it.

So capability elicitation matters because we want our evaluations to tell us something about what a motivated actor could actually accomplish with the model. We don’t want to mistake a failure of our evaluation setup for evidence of safety. And that doesn’t mean assuming every model has hidden dangerous abilities. It means being explicit about how much confidence a negative result really warrants.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Project Naptime, cyber tasks, or improved performance from a supportive environment.

r002.rationale: It says a failed evaluation may reflect the setup and urges caution about negative results, but does not state that a low result supports safety in the domain only after eliciting the model’s maximum capability.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that revealing a model’s full capabilities can take months of experimentation.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, what we care about is what a model could do if someone were really trying to get it to perform a dangerous task. And that’s not necessarily what you observe when you just ask it a question in a fairly straightforward way.

A model might have the relevant capabilities, but you need the right prompting, or tools, or scaffolding to bring them out. You might need to give it multiple attempts, or fine-tune it. So if your evaluation doesn’t do a good job of eliciting those capabilities, you can get a false sense of security: the model fails your test, but someone who puts more effort into using it could succeed.

There’s an important asymmetry here. If you demonstrate a dangerous capability, you’ve learned that the model can do it under those conditions. If you fail to demonstrate it, you don’t necessarily know whether the capability is absent or whether you just haven’t found a way to elicit it. So capability elicitation is central to how much confidence we should place in a negative evaluation result.

r002.rationale: It says negative results are less trustworthy if capabilities have not been elicited, but does not state that a safety conclusion in the evaluated domain requires eliciting the model’s maximum capability.

r003.rationale: The response mentions multiple attempts and fine-tuning but does not say that revealing full capabilities can take months of experimentation.
